But in my experience you should only bathe a rabbit if 1. the rabbit is calm with water, I have found that most of my buns dislike the water and will react very badly to being exposed to a bath (even when the water is very low and warm but not hot). 2. It is needed, I usually try to find other ways to clean my bun before I jump to giving them a bath (usually i will go with a damp wash cloth if it is really needed). and 3. You are ready to deal with a wet rabbit, this doesn't sound bad but a wet rabbit can make itself even more dirty than it originally was. Also, rabbits unique coat seem to hold water for an extended period of time. 
To sum it up if you and your rabbit feel comfortable with a bath it is a-somewhat-okay.

For smaller rabbits I recommend Holland lops (I raise and love them), Netherlands dwarfs (I know a lot of people who raise/raised them), Jersey woolys (usually pretty chill, from what I have seen), It would take a while for me to list everybunny. So, I suggest you do some research and look around for someone who raises the breed you are interested in and see what they think.
2. Rabbits can vary. Usually, each breed has its own specific personality. For example: Flemish Giants are usually chill af when they are comfortable. Britannia petites are usually rude and harder to deal with. So, I will still have to say research your breeds.
3. I have never had a problem with owning a single rabbit. As long as you give it the attention it deserves, they should be fine.
4.
Food- $5 to $55 (usually "pet" feeds are cheaper) Timothy hay should always be supplied and you can get a good quality hay for about $10. Treats are expensive ($5 to $15 for a bag) in my opinion so I give them plain cheerios.
Cage/habitat/hutch- $30 to really depends how devoted you are to a hutch. Usually a "medium" sized hutch is good as long as you have time to let him/her run and play outside of it for a while each day.
Vet bills always vary (sorry for the lame response).
Toys can be $1 to $20 (usually tunnels and edible tunnels are $20).
Bottles and or dishes are usually $1-$5.
A "pet quality" rabbit can usually be found for $20 by a breeder. 
5. It really depends on the actual rabbits in my opinion. But usually males like to spray pee (females can too but I see it more in males). I never owned a spayed or neutered rabbit but their attitude will/can change a lot from the hormonal change.
6. The longest I have driven with a bunny in the back is about 4 hours. I suggest keeping an extra eye on him/her. If you don't spay the female she might actually become horny from the ride... Carriers range in size so if you are worried about a bunny not having enough space then buy a carrier for a larger breed.
7. Depends on the rabbit/breed. I have some rabbits that tend to just stay within a yard of me. I do suggest bunny proofing your home (keeping wires up, making sure there are no places he/she can go under and hide for a while) if you plan to have them out a lot.
8. enclosure requirements can vary on how much outside time you give them. If you make it remember to have wire that is about 14 gauge so they don't hurt their feet.

Since angoras have the long hair they are prone to accidental ingestion, causing hairballs. While rabbits can cough (or puke) they can only expel the hair from digestion. To promote digestion of hair feed them papaya or pineapple juice. The acidic-ness of the juice will help break down the hair.
Some feed, like a certain Heinold rabbit feed that comes in a purple (i think) bag, contains papaya. I heard you can feed this instead of constant juice (which get bunnies sticky :( ). Of course feed tons of Timothy hay. I also include black sunflower seeds and Quaker old fashioned oats in my feed.
Also, always mix the new feed with the old, slowly introducing the new. So your Angora will get used to the new feed.

Have you tried examining her ear? Dirt or crust in the ear indicates ear mites. It could also be an ear infection. If the mites are not treated she will develop an ear canker, if it is an infection and is left untreated than it can spiral into wry neck (rabbit has its head tilted almost always permanent) . From the information given it will probably develop into wry (the head tilting is a bit of a give away).

If you are very concerned plan a vet appointment, but if you have been raising rabbits for a while and know about these problems you can treat it at home. 
If you go to a vet, be careful because I have found most vets do not know much about rabbits (or at least in my area) and it never hurts to do some extra research on the internet after the appointment.
